\[
B = \operatorname{bilateral}(\log_{10} I),
\quad
D = \log_{10} I - B,
\quad
O = c\,B + D - c \max B,
\quad
c = \frac{\log_{10} C}{\max B - \min B},
\qquad C = 5
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(I\): The intensity (20 R + 40 G + B) / 61
- \(B\): The base layer, the bilateral filter of log10 I
- \(D\): The detail layer
- \(C\): The target base contrast
- \(O\): The log10 of the output intensity

I is the intensity (20 R + 40 G + B) / 61. The bilateral filter of the log intensity is the base layer B, the large shapes of the light. What is left, D, is the detail. The base is scaled by c, so that its range becomes log10 C, and shifted so that its largest value becomes 0. The detail is not scaled, so it keeps its contrast. Each channel becomes its ratio to I times 10^O, clipped to 1. Durand and Dorsey keep sigma_s at 2 percent of the image size and found sigma_r = 0.4 and a base contrast of 5 to work well. The bilateral filter is their piecewise-linear version. It filters at NB evenly spaced levels of log I, with NB = (max - min) / sigma_r rounded up. Each pixel mixes the two levels nearest to its value. PixelNexus's own choices are linear light for 8-bit images, intensities of at least 1e-4, the longer side as the image size, and bilinear upsampling.
